title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit - Microsoft Research
gist: Microsoft Research and GitHub Next present PDD Kit, a research-prototype toolkit for 'Proof-Driven Development' that turns a developer's plain-language intent into a Verus formal spec, has coding agents write Rust code plus proofs, and falls back to labeled tests for a trusted boundary. Demonstrated on the login logic of a ~5,000-line Rust Pet Store app inside GitHub Next's Chopin, it shifts review from line-by-line code reading to intent review; the page credits authors Alex Lavaee and Matthai Philipose while the raw author field is Brenda Potts.

insights.claim: Microsoft Research argues that because coding agents now ship features spanning tens or hundreds of thousands of lines in one sitting, exhaustive line-by-line human review of pull requests no longer scales.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Verification and assurance tooling becomes a gating layer for enterprise adoption of agentic coding.
insights.locator: Coding agents now ship whole features

insights.claim: The post says agents drift from the natural-language plan and then write tests that pass for their own implementation rather than the intended behavior, so CI fills with high-quantity low-quality tests and healthy-looking coverage hides the gap.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Test coverage metrics become less trustworthy as AI-generated code grows, creating demand for stronger correctness guarantees.
insights.quote: The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for.

insights.claim: Formal proofs were historically too expensive for everyday software because they required specialists and proofs many times larger than the code, but coding agents can now help generate both formal specs and proofs, making Proof-Driven Development practical.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: LLMs could expand formal verification from niche (aerospace, crypto) to mainstream software, a new tooling market.
insights.quote: Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?”
insights.locator: Proofs used to be too expensive

insights.claim: PDD Kit runs inside GitHub Next's multiplayer planning environment Chopin, asks reviewer-style clarifying questions, records answers in an intent artifact, converts formalizable intent into Verus specs and the rest into informal specs for tests, and labels every result as proof or empirical evidence.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Microsoft/GitHub are building differentiated assurance features into their agentic developer stack.

insights.claim: Verus, the Rust proof language PDD Kit uses, is co-developed by Microsoft Research with Carnegie Mellon, VMware Research, ETH Zurich and other universities, and checks proofs deterministically via the Z3 solver with no model involved.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Deterministic checking provides an auditable guarantee that LLM self-review cannot.
insights.quote: Models write the spec, code, and proof, but only a deterministic Verus run decides whether it passed.

insights.claim: PDD Kit makes the Trusted Computing Base explicit: components the verifier cannot see, such as bcrypt hashing, sqlx queries, jsonwebtoken signing and the clock, are wrapped with assumed contracts that the developer accepts one by one and that receive tests.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Guarantees are bounded by third-party dependencies, so supply-chain assurance remains a separate need.

insights.claim: To guard against 'vibe verification' (weak invariants that verify but rule out almost nothing), PDD Kit's pdd-prove plants one bug per ensures clause and requires Verus to reject each mutant, while two reviewer agents and an LLM verifier check the spec and look for gaps.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Highlights that AI-generated proofs can be hollow; mutation testing is a key quality control investors should expect in such tools.
insights.quote: When a model writes its own spec, or is tuned to produce proofs, it tends to land on weak invariants: clauses that verify but rule out almost nothing.
insights.locator: Step 6: Prove, check, close the gaps

insights.claim: PDD Kit's pdd-ship workflow adds the Verus check to CI so any later change by a human or agent must keep proving against the same spec, and it prunes example-based tests made redundant by the proof, making CI both stronger and leaner.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Could reduce CI compute and test-maintenance costs while raising assurance.
insights.locator: Merging is where the proof joins

insights.claim: Verus proof checks typically take seconds for a small module and up to minutes for a larger codebase.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Verification latency is compatible with normal CI pipelines.

insights.claim: Microsoft tested PDD Kit on Pet Store, a roughly 5,000-line full-stack Rust app (Axum and SQLite backend, Leptos/WebAssembly storefront), formally verifying its login logic; the process hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, and the developer merged without reading the generated code line by line.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Early evidence that agent-generated formal verification works on real application code, not just toy examples.
insights.locator: The capstone: a full-stack web app

insights.claim: A two-sentence developer request ('You only get a token with the right password' and 'Only admin accounts get admin tokens') became eight ensures clauses on login_flow after PDD Kit surfaced that the first sentence alone would be satisfied by a login that refuses everyone.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Shows how agents silently resolve specification ambiguity, a hidden source of defects in AI-written code.
insights.quote: An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways.

insights.claim: The formal spec catches wiring bugs such as checking the password against one account but signing a token for another, a class of bug the authors say test suites rarely think to look for.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Formal methods target high-impact security bugs in auth and permissions where breaches are costly.
insights.locator: Notice that the same a appears

insights.claim: The authors acknowledge the login guarantees are only as strong as six trusted pieces, with check_password and the two database lookups carrying most of the weight, supported by tests but not proved.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: 'Fully verified' claims in the market should be scrutinized for their trusted boundaries.
insights.locator: What to Expect from PDD Kit

insights.claim: PDD Kit is a research prototype that verifies only Rust because Verus targets Rust; other-language code must be ported or call verified Rust through bindings, and proofs still take real effort.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Near-term adoption is limited and may reinforce Rust's position in security-critical code.

insights.claim: The authors argue that once line-by-line review is no longer the main safeguard, readability stops being the main reason to choose a language, so teams can pick languages for speed and safety and optimize aggressively since any spec-breaking change fails the proof.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Suggests AI plus verification could shift language choice toward performance-oriented languages.
insights.locator: There’s also a less obvious upside

insights.claim: Microsoft recommends starting verification where bugs cost the most, such as login, payments or permissions, and expects the trusted boundary to shrink significantly over time so more code can be formally verified.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Payments and identity code are the likely first commercial beachheads for AI-assisted formal verification.
insights.locator: What to Expect from PDD Kit
